metadata.title: Machine learning algorithm for grading open-ended physics questions in Turkish

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a university-level Turkish Physics short-answer dataset (four questions) with 246 undergraduate participants and does not describe any complex survey design or the use of sampling/survey weights. Because the analysis is based on supervised text classification with train/test splits and cross-validation, the manuscript does not report applying any student-level sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife). The weighting strategy therefore appears to be absent or not documented, and results should be interpreted as model performance on the collected course sample rather than population-representative estimates. Preprocessing includes Turkish text normalization, TF-IDF weighting, feature selection, and class balancing (SMOTE) before model training.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, it predicts expert-assigned categorical grades for four physics short-answer questions from student text. Because the dependent variables are discrete class labels derived from scoring keys (0/1, 0–4), PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy for student responses (e.g., how unanswered items or incomplete texts were handled), which is a reporting gap given that text-based pipelines typically require explicit rules for missing/empty responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 246 undergraduate students (age 19–22) who had taken a Turkish Physics course at state universities in Istanbul, Turkey. The study used four university-level physics short-answer questions; each student’s handwritten short responses were scored by three raters using an expert-determined scoring key. The analytic dataset was constructed per question (four separate datasets), then preprocessed and balanced (SMOTE) before splitting into 75% training and 25% testing sets with random partitioning repeated for ten iterations.

main_findings.dataset_used: Turkish university Physics short-answer grading (4 questions; Q1–Q4)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Turkish university Physics short-answer grading data (four expert-scored questions), the study leveraged Question (Q1–Q4) and Scoring categories (0–1/0–4) (with student background such as year in program and age) to predict the expert-assigned grade class from students’ Turkish short responses, finding that AdaBoost.M1 achieved the highest average accuracy and strong precision/F1 across all four questions. This indicates that boosting-based automatic scoring can approximate expert grading for Turkish physics short answers, supporting scalable, more objective feedback in national or university assessment settings, though the results are limited to this single-course dataset and do not establish causal validity.

data.outcome_summary: The study developed an automatic short-answer grading system for four university-level Turkish Physics questions using supervised text classification. The dataset comprised 246 undergraduate students in Istanbul, Turkey, with each question scored into discrete categories using an expert-determined scoring key; the model predicts these grade classes from students’ Turkish written responses. After Turkish text normalization, TF-IDF weighting, feature selection, and class balancing via SMOTE, the authors trained and compared SVM, Gini (decision tree), KNN, Bagging, and AdaBoost.M1 using 75%/25% train-test splits repeated for ten iterations plus k-fold cross-validation. AdaBoost.M1 was selected as best, with accuracy ranging from 0.84–0.99 (Q1) to 0.65–0.84 (Q2), and F1-score ranging from 0.77–0.97 depending on question. Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and no documentation of survey-weighting or representativeness beyond the single course sample.
